description: We’re Atlas Junior, a six-member student robotics team from Barishal, Bangladesh. We enjoy building robots, writing code, and using what we learn to create projects other students can try.For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we made Atlas SkyBase, a Mars outpost game where students drive a rover, scout rocky terrain, and manage limited power. We brought together our interests in robotics, 3D design, and space science to make a game that lets students see how one decision can change a full mission.
summary:
We made Atlas SkyBase, a browser game for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. We’re Atlas Junior, a robotics team from Barishal, Bangladesh. In our game, students drive a rover across rocky Martian terrain, scout observation points, and plan how to collect a sample and bring it back to base while keeping track of power, oxygen, water, and food.

We used archived NASA InSight air-temperature data from Sol 32 to model the habitat’s heating needs. When it gets colder, the habitat needs more power, leaving less for the rover. That gives students a decision to make: keep exploring, or turn back while they still have enough power to get home?

We made Atlas SkyBase so students could see how their choices affect a mission and practice planning together with limited resources.
details:
We made Atlas SkyBase, a browser-based Mars outpost game for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. We’re Atlas Junior, a robotics team from Barishal, Bangladesh. We wanted students to experience what it feels like to make decisions on Mars when the rover and the crew depend on the same limited power supply. Play Atlas SkyBase

How it works

The game has two rover missions. In Scout the Terrain, players steer around rocks to reach an observation point. In Collect and Cache, they plan a route to a sample site, collect a rock, and carry it back to the depot. The outpost display tracks power, oxygen, water, and food. A longer route may avoid rough terrain, but it can leave less power for the return trip.

We used NASA InSight’s archived Sol 32 air-temperature data in our outpost demonstration to show how cooling on Mars affects simulated heating demand. As the outside temperature drops, keeping the habitat warm takes more power. The temperature graph shows the NASA data, and the simulation shows the resulting heating demand in game units.

What we used

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser prototype. We created 3D visuals of the habitat, greenhouse, solar panels, batteries, and rover to show how the outpost’s systems fit together. An ESP32 controller is part of our planned physical extension. We want students to see a command on the computer turn on a model greenhouse light or move a rover.

Why we made it

We combined an outpost model with rover gameplay so students can see how a choice made at the base affects what they can do on the surface. We considered how to make the controls approachable, how to show resource changes clearly, and how to explain the difference between an archived temperature and a simulated heating value.

We designed Atlas SkyBase for students ages 7–12. In a classroom, students can share roles, discuss a route, and decide how much power to reserve before sending the rover out. Our goal is for them to practice teamwork and explain why they made a decision after seeing its consequences.

To know more about the project visit: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1w6hZYGCzlJF1073m9qfrpr5mF7CaNKBo?usp=sharing
